entry: American actor and environmental activist. Ford achieved global stardom as Han Solo in the space opera film *Star Wars* (1977) and reprised the role in four later films. He also played the title character in the *Indiana Jones* films and Rick Deckard in *Blade Runner*, becoming one of Hollywood's most bankable stars. His only Oscar nomination, for Best Actor, was for *Witness* (1985). He has also starred in the [[Western (genre)|western]] series *1923* and the comedy series *Shrinking*. Ford is a licensed pilot and has been vice chair of Conservation International since 1991.

[[Agriculture|Agricultural]] implement used for surface [[Tillage|tillage]]. It is used after [[Plough|ploughing]] to break up clods and smooth the soil into a structure called tilth, suitable for planting [[Seed|seeds]]. Coarser harrowing also removes weeds and covers seed after sowing. Unlike a plow, which cuts the upper 12 to 25 cm (5 to 10 in) of soil and leaves furrows, a harrow disturbs the whole surface. Disc harrows suit heavy work such as breaking up sod, while chain harrows suit lighter work such as leveling the tilth. Harrows were once drawn by draft animals but are now almost always attached to a [[Tractor|tractor]].

American singer, actor and civil rights activist. He popularized calypso internationally in the 1950s and 1960s. His album *Calypso* (1956) was the first million-selling LP by a single artist, and his best-known recording is "Day-O (The Banana Boat Song)". He starred in films including *Carmen Jones* (1954) and *Island in the Sun* (1957). He was a close confidant of [[Martin Luther King Jr.]] during the [[Civil rights movement|civil rights movement]] and a vocal critic of [[George W. Bush]] and the first Donald Trump administrations. He won three [[Grammy Awards|Grammys]], a Primetime Emmy and a Tony Award.

American escapologist, illusionist and stunt performer. Born Erik Weisz in [[Budapest]], then part of [[Austria-Hungary]], he emigrated to the [[United States]] as a child and first appeared in [[Vaudeville|vaudeville]] there. He took the stage name Harry Houdini after the French magician Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin. His escape acts included chains, straitjackets, nailed packing cases lowered under water and a sealed milk can, and in 1904 he attempted escape from special handcuffs commissioned by London's *Daily Mirror*, keeping crowds in suspense for an hour. He was also a critic of fraudulent spiritualist mediums, and in the 1920s he clashed with [[Arthur Conan Doyle]], a spiritualism advocate. He made several films but gave up acting when it failed to bring in money, and he was the first man to fly a powered aircraft in Australia. He died in [[Detroit]] of peritonitis caused by a ruptured appendix.

Series of seven fantasy novels by British author [[J. K. Rowling]]. The books follow the young wizard Harry Potter and his friends Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger at Hogwarts School of [[Witchcraft]] and Wizardry. The central conflict is between Harry and the dark wizard Lord Voldemort, who seeks immortality and control of the Ministry of Magic. Major themes include prejudice, corruption, madness, love and death. The first novel, *Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone*, was published on 26 June 1997, and by February 2023 the series had sold more than 600 million copies, the best-selling book series in history. The final instalment sold roughly 2.7 million copies in the United Kingdom and 8.3 million in the United States within twenty-four hours of its release. [[Warner Bros. Pictures]] adapted the books into an eight-part [[Harry Potter (film series)|film series]], and a television series is in production at [[HBO]].

Eight-film fantasy series based on the novels by [[J. K. Rowling]]. Produced and distributed by [[Warner Bros. Pictures]], it began with *Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone* (2001) and ended with *Deathly Hallows – Part 2* (2011). [[Daniel Radcliffe]], Rupert Grint and [[Emma Watson]] starred as Harry Potter, Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger. [[Steven Spielberg]] initially negotiated to direct the first film, but the deal was not finalized. *Deathly Hallows – Part 2* grossed $1.3 billion, and the series, with $7.7 billion in worldwide receipts, is the fourth-highest-grossing film series.

33rd [[President of the United States|president of the United States]], 1945–1953. As vice president, Truman succeeded [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]] when Roosevelt died in April 1945, and he was told about the Manhattan Project only then. He authorized the first and only wartime use of [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapons]], against [[Hiroshima]] and [[Nagasaki]]. He established the Truman Doctrine, set up the Marshall Plan to rebuild Western Europe and supported the founding of [[NATO]] to contain Soviet communism. The [[Cold War]] began during his presidency, and the United States entered the [[Korean War]] in 1950. Congress having refused civil rights legislation, Truman issued Executive Orders 9980 and 9981, prohibiting discrimination in federal agencies and desegregating the armed forces. He won the 1948 election against Republican Thomas E. Dewey and Dixiecrat Strom Thurmond, and he did not run in 1952 after poor polling. Historians consistently rank him in the first quartile of U.S. presidents.

Emperor of Kannauj, 606–647. After the decline of the [[Gupta Empire]], northern India was divided into several kingdoms, and Harsha succeeded his brother Rajyavardhana, king of Thanesar, who had been murdered by Shashanka, king of Gauda. Harsha ascended the throne at 16. At its height his realm covered much of northern India, with the Narmada River as its southern boundary. He made Kanyakubja, present-day Kannauj in [[Uttar Pradesh]], his imperial capital. His court attracted scholars and religious visitors, and the Chinese traveler [[Xuanzang]] praised his justice and generosity. Harsha was defeated by Pulakeshin II of the Chalukya dynasty at the Battle of Narmada when he tried to expand into southern India. His biography, *Harshacharita*, was written in [[Sanskrit]] by the poet Banabhatta.

City, capital of [[Connecticut]], U.S. (pop., 2020: 121,054). It is among the oldest cities in the United States. It is home to the country's oldest continuously operating public art museum, the Wadsworth Atheneum, and the [[Mark Twain]] House, where Twain wrote his most famous works. Hartford was the richest city in the United States for several decades after the [[American Civil War]], and it has been the sole capital of Connecticut since 1875. Nicknamed the "Insurance Capital of the World," it is the headquarters of many insurance companies, the region's major industry.

Primary international airport serving [[Atlanta]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]]. Named after former Atlanta mayors William B. Hartsfield and Maynard Jackson, it has been the world's busiest airport by passenger traffic since 1998, except in 2020, and served 106.3 million passengers in 2025. It is the primary hub of [[Delta Air Lines]], and Delta's hub, with just over 1,000 flights a day to 225 destinations, is the world's largest airline hub. Its longest of five parallel runways, 12,390 feet (3,776 m), can accommodate the [[Airbus A380]]. The airport covers 4,700 acres (19 sq km).

Japanese novelist and short-story writer. Born in [[Kyoto]] and raised in [[Kobe]], he ran a jazz bar in [[Tokyo]] before publishing his first novel, *Hear the Wind Sing* (1979). His works, including *Norwegian Wood* (1987), *Kafka on the Shore* (2002) and *1Q84* (2009–10), have been translated into more than 50 languages and have sold millions of copies outside Japan. Blending [[Science fiction|science fiction]], fantasy and magical realism, his fiction draws on Western writers such as [[Franz Kafka]], [[Kurt Vonnegut]] and [[Raymond Chandler]]. His nonfiction includes *Underground* (1997), an oral history of the [[Tokyo subway sarin attack]], and *What I Talk About When I Talk About Running* (2007). His fiction has polarized critics, and some in Japan's literary establishment have called it un-Japanese.

Fifth Abbasid caliph, 786–809. His reign is traditionally regarded as the beginning of the [[Islamic Golden Age]], and [[Baghdad]] flourished as a world center of knowledge, culture and trade. He established the library [[House of Wisdom|Bayt al-Hikma]] there. In 796 he moved his court to Raqqa in present-day [[Syria]]. Under him the Abbasid Empire reached its peak, and large-scale hostilities broke out with [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantium]]. In 799 a Frankish mission brought him friendship, and he sent presents to [[Charlemagne]], including a clock that Charlemagne and his retinue deemed a conjuration. Portions of the fictional work *One Thousand and One Nights* are set in his court.

Private [[Ivy League]] research university in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts|Cambridge]], Massachusetts. Founded in 1636, it is the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States. It was named Harvard College in 1639 after its first benefactor, the Puritan clergyman John Harvard, and in 1638 it acquired English North America's first known [[Printing press|printing press]]. Under president Charles William Eliot from 1869 to 1909, it developed professional schools and became a modern research university. James B. Conant led it through the [[Great Depression]] and [[World War II]]. Its library holds more than 20 million volumes, the largest of any academic library in the world. Its alumni include eight U.S. presidents, among them [[John Adams]] and [[Barack Obama]].

Process of gathering mature crops from fields. The word comes from Old English *hærfest*, meaning autumn, and "harvest" also refers to the collected crops. Harvesting also collects plants, animals and fish as food, and on small farms with little mechanization it is the most labor-intensive activity of the growing season. On large farms a [[Combine harvester|combine harvester]] does the work, while reaping grain typically used a [[Sickle|sickle]], scythe or reaper. Completion of the harvest marks the end of the growing season and is the focus of seasonal [[Harvest festival|harvest festivals]]. Crop failure, caused by drought, storms, floods or soil degradation, has triggered [[Famine|famines]] and [[Human migration|human migration]] throughout history. The term also applies to fishing and logging, and to harvesting grapes for wine.

Annual celebration around the time of a region's main [[Harvest|harvest]]. Harvest festivals typically feature feasting with foods drawn from the crops. In Britain, thanks have been given for harvests since pagan times, and modern celebrations include singing [[Hymn|hymns]], [[Prayer|prayer]] and decorating [[Church (building)|churches]] with baskets of fruit and food. Produce is often distributed to the poor or used to raise funds for charity. In [[Ethiopia]], the Oromo celebrate Irreecha, which marks the end of the rainy season. In India, Makar Sankranti, Thai Pongal, [[Holi]] and Onam are among the harvest festivals. [[Jews]] celebrate the week-long Sukkot in autumn, living in a temporary hut called a sukkah, which is reminiscent of the tabernacles Israelite farmers lived in during the harvest. The Chinese Mid-Autumn Festival is one of the most widely spread harvest festivals in the world.

American politician and gay rights activist. Raised on [[Long Island]], he served in the U.S. Navy during the [[Korean War]] before moving to [[San Francisco]] in 1972 and opening a camera store. He was elected to the San Francisco Board of Supervisors in 1977, becoming the first openly gay man elected to public office in California. Milk sponsored a bill banning discrimination based on sexual orientation in public accommodations, housing and employment, and the supervisors passed it 11–1. Milk and Mayor George Moscone were assassinated by Dan White, a former supervisor who had cast the sole vote against the bill. Milk became a martyr in the LGBTQ community and was posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2009.

American former film producer and convicted sex offender. He co-founded Miramax and The Weinstein Company, whose films grossed over $10.78 billion worldwide. More than 80 women made harassment or rape allegations against him in 2017, sparking the [[MeToo movement|MeToo]] campaign. He was convicted in New York and Los Angeles. A 2020 New York sentence of 23 years was overturned on appeal in 2024 for procedural errors, and a 2025 retrial produced a mixed verdict. In September 2026 he was sentenced to 15 years in prison. Some allegations did not lead to convictions.

State in northwestern India. Formed on 1 November 1966 out of [[Punjab]], it shares its capital, [[Chandigarh]], with the neighboring state. It surrounds [[Delhi]] on three sides, and much of its land lies within the National Capital Region. Rakhigarhi and Bhirrana are sites of the [[Indus Valley Civilisation|Indus Valley Civilisation]]. In the Vedic era the area was home to the Kuru kingdom, and Kurukshetra, the battlefield of the [[Mahabharata]], lies in the state. The [[Yamuna]] river forms its eastern border. Haryana's economy is the 13th largest in India, and it ranks 11th among Indian states in the [[Human Development Index]].

[[Data structure|Data structure]] that maps keys to values using a hash function. The function computes an index into an array of buckets. Most designs use an imperfect hash function, so collisions are handled by separate chaining or open addressing. In a well-dimensioned table, average lookup time is independent of the number of stored elements. Built-in versions include [[Python (programming language)|Python]]'s dictionaries and [[Java (programming language)|Java]]'s HashMap, and hash tables are widely used for database indexing and caches. In January 1953, Hans Peter Luhn wrote an internal [[IBM]] memorandum using hashing with chaining.

Metadata tag prefixed with the symbol #. On [[Social media|social media]] it groups posts by topic, so that a search for #flowers on [[Instagram]] returns every post tagged with that term. American blogger Chris Messina proposed the convention in a 2007 tweet, and it became entrenched on Twitter and spread to Instagram, Facebook and [[YouTube]]. The number sign had earlier appeared in the [[C (programming language)|C]] programming language and in IRC channel names. In June 2014 the [[Oxford English Dictionary]] added hashtag as a word. Critics argue that hashtag activism often amounts to low-effort signaling, though proponents say it lowers barriers to participation.

Religious movement within [[Judaism]]. Founded by Israel ben Eliezer, known as the [[Baal Shem Tov]], it arose in Western Ukraine in the 18th century and spread through Eastern Europe. Its teachings draw on [[Kabbalah|Lurianic Kabbalah]] and stress God's immanence in the universe and the need to be one with God at all times. Hasidim are organized into dynasties, each led by a hereditary Rebbe to whom followers show reverence and submission. Present-day Hasidism is a subgroup of [[Haredi Judaism]], known for religious conservatism, distinctive dress and the [[Yiddish]] language. As of 2015 there were roughly 250,000 followers worldwide, about 2% of the global Jewish population.

Sultan of Brunei since 1967 and prime minister since 1984. He is the 29th sultan of Brunei, the world's longest-reigning current monarch and one of the few remaining absolute monarchs. He holds executive, legislative and judicial powers under the Malay Islamic Monarchy system. He studied in [[Kuala Lumpur]] at Victoria Institution from 1961 to 1963 and was the first sultan of Brunei to complete his education both domestically and abroad. Brunei's [[Sharia]] penal code, phased in from 2014 and fully enforced in 2019, includes [[Amputation|amputation]] for theft and death for [[Homosexuality|homosexuality]] among Muslims, which has drawn international human rights criticism.

First president of [[Malawi]], 1966–1994. Banda led the country to independence in 1964 after returning from abroad to campaign against [[Colonialism|colonial]] rule, and in 1966 he proclaimed Malawi a [[Republic|republic]] with himself as president. He established a one-party state under the Malawi Congress Party and became president for life in 1971. A renowned anti-communist, he received Western support during the [[Cold War]] and maintained full diplomatic relations with the [[Apartheid|apartheid]] government of [[South Africa]]. He generally supported [[Women's rights|women's rights]] and improved the country's infrastructure. His rule has been characterized as a highly repressive [[Autocracy|autocracy]], and human rights groups estimate that at least 6,000 people were killed, tortured or jailed without trial. By 1993 he agreed to a referendum ending the one-party system, and he lost the multiparty election that followed. He died in South Africa.

Shaped head covering worn for protection, ceremony, religion or fashion. In the past hats indicated social status, and in the [[Military|military]] they may denote nationality, branch of service, rank or regiment. Some hats protect the wearer, such as the hard hat for construction workers and the sun hat that shades the face and shoulders. Hats were probably commonplace before 3,000 BC. A [[Bronze Age]] man nicknamed Ötzi, found frozen in a mountain between Austria and Italy, wore a bearskin cap. A tomb painting at [[Thebes, Egypt|Thebes]] shows a man in a conical straw hat from around 3200 BC. In the Middle Ages, the 1215 Fourth Council of the Lateran required Jews to wear a Judenhat, usually yellow, which marked them as targets for [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]]. The word milliner comes from [[Milan]], where the best hats were made in the 18th century.

Major goddess in [[Ancient Egyptian religion|ancient Egyptian religion]]. As a sky deity, Hathor was the mother or consort of the sky god Horus and the sun god [[Ra]], making her the symbolic mother of the [[Pharaoh|pharaohs]]. Her beneficent side represented beauty, music, joy, love and maternal care, while as the Eye of Ra she had a vengeful aspect. She was often depicted as a cow or as a woman wearing cow horns and a sun disk, and she helped the dead in the [[Afterlife|afterlife]]. More temples were dedicated to her than to any other goddess, with her most prominent temple at Dendera in Upper Egypt. The Egyptians linked her with foreign lands such as [[Nubia]] and [[Canaan]]. Women desiring children often invoked her in private prayers. After the New Kingdom she was overshadowed by [[Isis]], but she was venerated until the extinction of ancient Egyptian religion.
